concepts: Centroid, orthocentre and circumcentre (Euler line)
Infinite geometric series
questions.question: Points $O, A, B, C, \ldots$ are shown in the figure where $OA = 2AB = 4BC = \ldots$ and so on. Let $A$ be the centroid of a triangle whose orthocentre and circumcentre are $(2,4)$ and $\left(\frac{7}{2},\frac{5}{2}\right)$ respectively. An insect starts from $O(0,0)$ and moves along straight segments in zig-zag fashion (every segment makes $45^\circ$ with the $x$-axis: $O\to A$ upward, $A\to B$ downward, $B\to C$ upward, and so on) and finally terminates at the point $P(\alpha,\beta)$. Find the value of $(\alpha+\beta)$.
questions.key_idea: The centroid divides the orthocentre–circumcentre segment $2:1$, and each $45^\circ$ segment adds a geometric-series step to $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
solution: The centroid $G$ divides the line joining the orthocentre $H(2,4)$ and circumcentre $O\left(\frac72,\frac52\right)$ in the ratio $HG:GO = 2:1$.
So $G=\frac{H+2S}{3}\equiv\left(\frac{7+2}{3},\frac{5+4}{3}\right)=(3,3)$, where $S\left(\frac72,\frac52\right)$ is the circumcentre.
Since $A$ is the centroid, $A=(3,3)$ and $OA=3\sqrt2$ (the segment $OA$ makes $45^\circ$ with the $x$-axis).
The segments are $OA=3\sqrt2,\ AB=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2},\ BC=\frac{3\sqrt2}{4},\dots$ and each makes $45^\circ$, so each contributes (length)$\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ to the horizontal motion.
All horizontal moves are to the right: $\alpha=\frac{3\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}+\frac{3\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}+\frac{3\sqrt2}{4\sqrt2}+\cdots\infty=\dfrac{3}{1-\frac12}=6$.
The vertical moves alternate up and down: $\beta=\frac{3\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}+\frac{3\sqrt2}{4\sqrt2}-\cdots\infty=\dfrac{3}{1+\frac12}=2$.
Hence $\alpha+\beta=6+2=8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Self-similarity: the path after $A$ is the whole path scaled by $\frac12$ and reflected in the $x$-axis, so $P$ satisfies a fixed-point equation.
solution: As before $G=A=(3,3)$ (Euler line: $G=\frac{H+2S}{3}$ with circumcentre $S$).
After reaching $A$, the insect repeats the same zig-zag, but every length is halved and it first goes down instead of up (a reflection in a horizontal line).
So the displacement $P-A$ equals the displacement $P-O$ with the $x$-part halved and the $y$-part halved and reversed: $P-A=\left(\frac{\alpha}{2},-\frac{\beta}{2}\right)$.
$x$-part: $\alpha-3=\frac{\alpha}{2}\Rightarrow \alpha=6$.
$y$-part: $\beta-3=-\frac{\beta}{2}\Rightarrow \frac{3\beta}{2}=3\Rightarrow\beta=2$.
Hence $\alpha+\beta=8$ (no series needed).

useful_results: Euler line: $H$, $G$, $S$ (circumcentre) are collinear with $HG:GS=2:1$, so $G=\frac{H+2S}{3}$ and $H=3G-2S$.
A self-similar infinite path with ratio $r$ ($|r|<1$) has limit point $P$ satisfying $P=A+r\,\mathcal R(P)$; solve the fixed-point equation instead of summing a series.
A $45^\circ$ zig-zag with segment lengths in G.P. ratio $r$ gives $\alpha=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ and $\beta=\dfrac{a}{1+r}$ when the vertical moves alternate in sign (here $a=3$, $r=\frac12$).

concepts: Orthocentre and circumcentre of a triangle; reflection of a point in a line; medians
questions.question: The equations of the perpendiculars from $C$ to $AB$ and from $B$ to $AC$ of triangle $ABC$ (i.e. the lines perpendicular to the sides $AB$ and $AC$) are $x-y-4=0$ and $2x-y-5=0$ respectively. If the vertex $A$ is $(-2,3)$ and the point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors is $\left(\frac32,\frac52\right)$, find the equations of the medians to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ respectively.
questions.key_idea: The perpendicular bisector of a side is parallel to the altitude to the other side's normal, so $B$ and $C$ are mirror images of $A$ in the two perpendicular bisectors.
solution: The two given perpendiculars are altitudes; they meet at the orthocentre: solving $x-y-4=0$, $2x-y-5=0$ gives $x=1,\ y=-3$, so $H=(1,-3)$.

The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is perpendicular to $AB$, hence parallel to the line $x-y-4=0$ (which is also perpendicular to $AB$); it passes through the circumcentre $\left(\frac32,\frac52\right)$, so it is $x-y+1=0$.
Similarly the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ is parallel to $2x-y-5=0$ and passes through the circumcentre: $2x-y-\frac12=0$, i.e. $4x-2y-1=0$.
$B$ is the image of $A(-2,3)$ in the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, $x-y+1=0$: $\frac{x+2}{1}=\frac{y-3}{-1}=-2\cdot\frac{-2-3+1}{2}=4$, so $B=(2,-1)$.
$C$ is the image of $A(-2,3)$ in the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, $4x-2y-1=0$: $\frac{x+2}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-2}=-2\cdot\frac{-8-6-1}{20}=\frac32$, so $C=(4,0)$.
(Check: $C$ lies on $x-y-4=0$ and $B$ lies on $2x-y-5=0$, as they must.)
Midpoint of $AB$ is $F=(0,1)$ and midpoint of $AC$ is $E=\left(1,\frac32\right)$.
Median to $AB$ is $CF$ with $C(4,0)$, $F(0,1)$: $y-0=\frac{1-0}{0-4}(x-4)\Rightarrow x+4y=4$.
Median to $AC$ is $BE$ with $B(2,-1)$, $E\left(1,\frac32\right)$: $y+1=\frac{\frac32+1}{1-2}(x-2)\Rightarrow 2y+2=-5x+10\Rightarrow 5x+2y=8$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF applies each perpendicular bisector to the wrong vertex: it finds $B=(4,0)$ from the bisector of $AC$ and $C=(2,-1)$ from the bisector of $AB$, i.e. $B$ and $C$ are interchanged. Correct: $B=(2,-1)$, $C=(4,0)$. Consequently the median to $AB$ is $CF$: $x+4y=4$ and the median to $AC$ is $BE$: $5x+2y=8$ (the PDF's labels CF and BE give the two equations in the opposite order, although the key lists them in the correct order).

alternate_solutions.idea: Euler's relation $H=A+B+C-2S$ gives $B+C$ at once; with $B,C$ on their altitudes the vertices follow from two linear equations.
solution: Let $S=\left(\frac32,\frac52\right)$ be the circumcentre and $H=(1,-3)$ the orthocentre (intersection of the two given altitudes).
Euler relation (vectors): $\vec H=\vec A+\vec B+\vec C-2\vec S$, so $\vec B+\vec C=\vec H+2\vec S-\vec A=(1,-3)+(3,5)-(-2,3)=(6,-1)$.
$C$ lies on the altitude from $C$: $x-y-4=0$, so $C=(q,q-4)$; $B$ lies on the altitude from $B$: $2x-y-5=0$, so $B=(p,2p-5)$.
Midpoints $F(0,1)$ of $AB$, $E\left(1,\frac32\right)$ of $AC$; medians $CF:\ x+4y=4$ and $BE:\ 5x+2y=8$.

useful_results: Euler relation: $H=A+B+C-2S$ (and $H=A+B+C$ if the circumcentre is the origin) — gives the sum of two unknown vertices from $A$, $H$, $S$.
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is parallel to the altitude through $C$ (both are $\perp AB$); the circumcentre then fixes its constant term.
Image of $(x_1,y_1)$ in $ax+by+c=0$: $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=-\frac{2(ax_1+by_1+c)}{a^2+b^2}$.

concepts: Incentre and internal angle bisector of a triangle
questions.question: The interior angle bisector of angle $A$ for the triangle $ABC$ whose vertices are $A(-8,5)$, $B(-15,-19)$ and $C(1,-7)$ has the equation $ax+2y+c=0$. Find $a$ and $c$.
questions.key_idea: The incentre $\left(\frac{ax_1+bx_2+cx_3}{a+b+c},\dots\right)$ lies on the bisector from $A$, so two points determine it.
solution: The incentre $I$ lies on the internal bisector of $A$. The side lengths are $a=BC=\sqrt{16^2+12^2}=20$.
Incentre: $I=\left(\frac{ax_1+bx_2+cx_3}{a+b+c},\frac{ay_1+by_2+cy_3}{a+b+c}\right)=\left(\frac{-160-225+25}{60},\frac{100-285-175}{60}\right)$.
$11x+2y+78=0$; comparing with $ax+2y+c=0$ gives $a=11$ and $c=78$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The internal bisector direction at $A$ is the sum of the unit vectors along $AB$ and $AC$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-7,-24)$ with $|AB|=25$, so the unit vector is $\left(-\frac{7}{25},-\frac{24}{25}\right)$.
$\overrightarrow{AC}=(9,-12)$ with $|AC|=15$, so the unit vector is $\left(\frac35,-\frac45\right)=\left(\frac{15}{25},-\frac{20}{25}\right)$.
The sum is $\left(\frac{8}{25},-\frac{44}{25}\right)\parallel(2,-11)$, so the bisector has slope $-\frac{11}{2}$.
Through $A(-8,5)$: $y-5=-\frac{11}{2}(x+8)\Rightarrow 2y-10=-11x-88\Rightarrow 11x+2y+78=0$.
So $a=11$, $c=78$ (matches).

useful_results: Internal bisector at $A$ has direction $\hat u_{AB}+\hat u_{AC}$ (sum of unit vectors); the external bisector has direction $\hat u_{AB}-\hat u_{AC}$.
Angle-bisector theorem: the bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $BD:DC=AB:AC$ (here $25:15=5:3$, $D=(-5,-11.5)$ lies on $11x+2y+78=0$).
Recognise Pythagorean triples: $20^2+15^2=25^2$, so the triangle is right-angled at $C$ and $r=\frac{a+b-c}{2}=5$.

concepts: Rhombus and its diagonals; angle bisectors of two lines
questions.question: Two sides of a rhombus $ABCD$ are parallel to the lines $y=x+2$ and $y=7x+3$. If the diagonals of the rhombus intersect at the point $(1,2)$ and the vertex $A$ is on the $y$-axis, find the possible coordinates of $A$.
questions.key_idea: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect the angles between its sides, so they are parallel to the angle bisectors of the two given directions.
solution: Let $A=(0,\alpha)$ and let $E=(1,2)$ be the intersection of the diagonals. Diagonals of a rhombus are parallel to the angle bisectors of the lines $y=x+2$ and $y=7x+3$.
Angle bisectors: $\frac{x-y+2}{\sqrt2}=\pm\frac{7x-y+3}{5\sqrt2}$.
With $(+)$: $5x-5y+10=7x-y+3\Rightarrow 2x+4y-7=0$, i.e. $x+2y-\frac72=0$ (slope $-\frac12$).
The diagonal $AE$ has slope equal to one of these: $m_{AE}=\frac{2-\alpha}{1-0}$.
If $m_{AE}=-\frac12$: $2-\alpha=-\frac12\Rightarrow\alpha=\frac52$.
If $m_{AE}=2$: $2-\alpha=2\Rightarrow\alpha=0$.
Hence $A=\left(0,\frac52\right)$ or $(0,0)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The centre of a rhombus is equidistant from all four sides, so $E$ is equidistant from the two sides through $A$.
solution: The sides through $A=(0,\alpha)$ are parallel to the given lines: $y=x+\alpha$ and $y=7x+\alpha$.
Distance of $E(1,2)$ from $x-y+\alpha=0$ is $\frac{|1-2+\alpha|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{|\alpha-1|}{\sqrt2}$.
Distance of $E(1,2)$ from $7x-y+\alpha=0$ is $\frac{|7-2+\alpha|}{5\sqrt2}=\frac{|\alpha+5|}{5\sqrt2}$.
Equal distances: $5|\alpha-1|=|\alpha+5|$.
Case $5(\alpha-1)=\alpha+5$ gives $\alpha=\frac52$; case $5(\alpha-1)=-(\alpha+5)$ gives $\alpha=0$.
So $A=(0,0)$ or $\left(0,\frac52\right)$ (matches).

useful_results: A parallelogram is a rhombus iff its diagonals bisect the angles at the vertices; its centre is equidistant from all four sides (incircle).

Bisectors of $a_1x+b_1y+c_1=0$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2=0$: $\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2}}=\pm\frac{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2}}$; the two bisector slopes here ($-\frac12$ and $2$) multiply to $-1$, as bisectors must.
Given only directions of the sides and the centre, the rhombus has one free parameter (its size); a condition such as 'A on the y-axis' fixes it (two solutions, one per diagonal).

concepts: Incentre and inradius; region of points nearer to one side of a triangle
questions.question: Let $O(0,0)$, $A(6,0)$ and $B(3,\sqrt3)$ be the vertices of $\triangle OAB$. Let $R$ be the region consisting of all those points $P$ inside $\triangle OAB$ which satisfy $d(P,OA)\le\min\{d(P,OB),\,d(P,AB)\}$, where $d(P,OA)$, $d(P,OB)$ and $d(P,AB)$ represent the distance of $P$ from the sides $OA$, $OB$ and $AB$ respectively. If the area of region $R$ is $9\left(a-\sqrt b\right)$ where $a$ and $b$ are coprime, then find the value of $(a+b)$.
questions.key_idea: Equal-distance conditions are angle bisectors, so $R$ is the triangle formed by $OA$ and the bisectors from $O$ and $A$ meeting at the incentre.
solution: $OB=2\sqrt3$, $AB=2\sqrt3$, $OA=6$; lines $OB:\ \sqrt3y=x$ and $AB:\ \sqrt3y=-x+6$; angles at $O$ and $A$ are $30^\circ$.
$d(P,OA)\le d(P,OB)$ means $P$ lies on the $OA$-side of the bisector of angle $O$; $d(P,OA)\le d(P,AB)$ means $P$ lies on the $OA$-side of the bisector of angle $A$.
These two bisectors meet at the incentre $I$, so $R$ is the triangle $OAI$.
Incentre: $I=\left(\frac{18+0+12\sqrt3}{6+4\sqrt3},\frac{6\sqrt3+0+0}{6+4\sqrt3}\right)$ (weights $2\sqrt3,2\sqrt3,6$ at $O,A,B$).
Height of $I$ above $OA$ is the inradius $r=\frac{6\sqrt3}{6+4\sqrt3}$.
Area of $R=\frac12\times6\times\frac{6\sqrt3}{6+4\sqrt3}=\frac{9\sqrt3}{3+2\sqrt3}$.
Rationalise: $\frac{9\sqrt3}{3+2\sqrt3}=9\cdot\frac{\sqrt3\,(2\sqrt3-3)}{3}=9\left(2-\sqrt3\right)$.
So $a=2$, $b=3$ (coprime) and $a+b=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The incentre splits the triangle into three triangles whose areas are proportional to the sides they stand on, so $[OAI]=[OAB]\cdot\frac{OA}{\text{perimeter}}$.
solution: Inradius $r$: $[OAI]=\frac12\,OA\cdot r$, $[OBI]=\frac12\,OB\cdot r$, $[ABI]=\frac12\,AB\cdot r$.
Adding, $[OAB]=\frac r2\,(OA+OB+AB)$, hence $\dfrac{[OAI]}{[OAB]}=\dfrac{OA}{OA+OB+AB}=\dfrac{6}{6+4\sqrt3}$.
$[OAB]=\frac12\cdot6\cdot\sqrt3=3\sqrt3$.
$[R]=3\sqrt3\cdot\frac{6}{6+4\sqrt3}=\frac{9\sqrt3}{3+2\sqrt3}=9(2-\sqrt3)$.
So $a+b=2+3=5$ (matches).

useful_results: The set of points of a triangle nearer to side $a$ than to the other two sides is the triangle formed by side $a$ and the two angle bisectors on it, meeting at the incentre.
The three such regions partition the triangle; their areas are in the ratio of the sides: $[R_a]:[R_b]:[R_c]=a:b:c$.
$r=\frac{\Delta}{s}$; here $\Delta=3\sqrt3$, $s=3+2\sqrt3$, $r=6-3\sqrt3\approx0.80$.

concepts: Angle bisectors and reflection of a point in a line; equations of the sides of a triangle
questions.question: Find the equations of the sides of a triangle having $(4,-1)$ as a vertex, if the lines $x-1=0$ and $x-y-1=0$ are the equations of two internal bisectors of its angles.
questions.key_idea: The mirror image of a vertex in the bisector of another vertex lies on the side opposite to the first vertex.
solution: Let $P(4,-1)$ be the vertex and let $Q,R$ be the other vertices, lying on $x=1$ and $x-y=1$ respectively.
The reflection of a vertex in the angle bisector of another vertex lies on the side opposite to the first vertex, so the reflections $B$ and $C$ of $P$ in $x=1$ and in $x-y=1$ lie on the side $QR$.
Reflection of $(4,-1)$ about $x=1$: $\frac{x_1+4}{2}=1\Rightarrow x_1=-2$ and $y_1=-1$, so $B=(-2,-1)$.
Reflection about $x-y-1=0$, $C=(x_2,y_2)$: the midpoint $\left(\frac{x_2+4}{2},\frac{y_2-1}{2}\right)$ lies on the line, giving $x_2-y_2+3=0$ (i).
The slope of $PC$ is $\frac{y_2+1}{x_2-4}$ and it is perpendicular to the line (slope $1$): $x_2+y_2-3=0$ (ii).
Solving (i) and (ii): $C=(0,3)$.
Equation of $BC$ (the side $QR$): $y+1=\frac42(x+2)\Rightarrow 2x-y+3=0$.
$Q$ lies on $x=1$ and on $BC$: $Q=(1,5)$; the side $PQ$ is $2x+y-7=0$.
$R$ lies on $x-y=1$ and on $BC$: $R=(-4,-5)$; the side $PR$ is $x-2y-6=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Symmetry of side slopes about a bisector: about the vertical line the slopes are $m,-m$; about a slope-$1$ line they are $m,\frac1m$.
solution: Let $Q=(1,q)$ (on $x=1$) and $R=(s,s-1)$ (on $x-y=1$); let the side $QR$ have slope $\mu$.
At $Q$ the bisector is vertical, so the sides $QP$ and $QR$ have slopes $m$ and $-m$: slope of $QP=-\mu$, i.e. $\frac{-1-q}{3}=-\mu$, so $q=3\mu-1$.
At $R$ the bisector has slope $1$; reflection in a slope-$1$ line sends slope $m$ to $\frac1m$, so slope of $RP=\frac1\mu$: $\frac{-1-(s-1)}{4-s}=\frac1\mu\Rightarrow\mu=\frac{s-4}{s}$.
Slope of $QR$: $\frac{s-1-q}{s-1}=\mu\Rightarrow s-1-(3\mu-1)=\mu(s-1)\Rightarrow\mu(s+2)=s$.
Substitute $\mu=\frac{s-4}{s}$: $(s-4)(s+2)=s^2\Rightarrow-2s-8=0\Rightarrow s=-4$, so $\mu=2$, $q=5$.

useful_results: Reflecting one side in the bisector at a vertex gives the other side at that vertex; hence the mirror image of a vertex in another vertex's bisector lies on the opposite side.
Reflection in a line parallel to an axis: about $x=k$ slopes $m\to-m$; about $y=x+c$ slopes $m\to\frac1m$.
The two given bisectors meet at the incentre $I=(1,0)$; the third bisector is $PI$ with slope $-\frac13$ (it bisects the angle between $PQ$ and $PR$ of slopes $-2$ and $\frac12$).

concepts: Locus of a point on a variable line through a fixed point
Harmonic progression
questions.question: $P$ is the point $(-1,2)$. A variable line through $P$ cuts the $x$ and $y$ axes at $A$ and $B$ respectively. $Q$ is the point on $AB$ such that $PA,\ PQ,\ PB$ are in H.P. Find the locus of $Q$.
questions.key_idea: Use signed distances from $P$ along the line: H.P. means $\frac{2}{PQ}=\frac1{PA}+\frac1{PB}$, and $x=h+\ldots,\ y=k+\ldots$ turns it into a linear relation in $h,k$.
solution: Let the line through $P(-1,2)$ make angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis and let $PA=r_1$, $PQ=r_2$, $PB=r_3$ be distances along it.
$Q(h,k)=(-1+r_2\cos\theta,\ 2+r_2\sin\theta)$.
$A(-1+r_1\cos\theta,\ 2+r_1\sin\theta)$ is on the $x$-axis: $2+r_1\sin\theta=0\Rightarrow r_1=\frac{-2}{\sin\theta}$.
$B(-1+r_3\cos\theta,\ 2+r_3\sin\theta)$ is on the $y$-axis: $-1+r_3\cos\theta=0\Rightarrow r_3=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}$.
$PA,PQ,PB$ in H.P.: $\frac{2}{r_2}=\frac1{r_1}+\frac1{r_3}=\frac{-\sin\theta}{2}+\frac{\cos\theta}{1}$.
Multiply by $r_2$: $2=\frac{-r_2\sin\theta}{2}+r_2\cos\theta$, and use $r_2\sin\theta=k-2$, $r_2\cos\theta=h+1$.
$4=-(k-2)+2(h+1)\Rightarrow 2h-k=0$.
Hence the locus of $Q$ is $y=2x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: H.P. means $Q$ is the harmonic conjugate of $P$ with respect to $A,B$, so $Q$ lies on the polar of $P$ with respect to the axes $xy=0$.
solution: $\frac{2}{PQ}=\frac1{PA}+\frac1{PB}$ (signed distances) says exactly that $A,B$ divide $PQ$ harmonically: $Q$ is the harmonic conjugate of $P$ with respect to $A$ and $B$.
$A$ and $B$ are the points where the line meets the pair of axes $xy=0$, so the locus of harmonic conjugates of $P(x_1,y_1)$ is the polar of $P$ with respect to this pair of lines.
The polar of $(x_1,y_1)$ with respect to $xy=0$ is $xy_1+yx_1=0$.
For $P(-1,2)$: $2x-y=0$, i.e. $y=2x$ (matches).

useful_results: For points on a line through $P$ (signed distances): $PA,PQ,PB$ in H.P. $\iff\frac2{PQ}=\frac1{PA}+\frac1{PB}\iff Q$ is the harmonic conjugate of $P$ w.r.t. $A,B$.
The locus of harmonic conjugates of $P$ w.r.t. the intersections of a variable line with a conic (or line pair $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$) is the polar of $P$: $axx_1+h(xy_1+yx_1)+byy_1=0$.
Numerical check: the line $y=x+3$ gives $A(-3,0)$, $B(0,3)$ and $Q=(3,6)$, which satisfies $y=2x$.

concepts: Orthocentre, altitudes and centroid of a triangle; locus
questions.question: The equations of the altitudes $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ of a triangle $ABC$ are $x+y=0$, $x-4y=0$ and $2x-y=0$ respectively. The coordinates of $A$ are $(t,-t)$. Find the coordinates of $B$ and $C$. Prove that if $t$ varies, the locus of the centroid of the triangle $ABC$ is $x+5y=0$.
questions.key_idea: $B$ lies on $x-4y=0$, $C$ on $2x-y=0$, and each of $AB,AC$ is perpendicular to the altitude through the third vertex.
solution: $B$ lies on $x-4y=0$: take $B=(4\alpha,\alpha)$; $C$ lies on $2x-y=0$: take $C=(b,2b)$.
$AB\perp CF$ (slope of $CF$ is $2$), so slope of $AB=-\frac12$: $\frac{-t-\alpha}{t-4\alpha}=\frac{-1}{2}$.
Cross-multiplying: $2t+2\alpha=t-4\alpha$, so $t=-6\alpha$ and $\alpha=-\frac t6$.
$AC\perp BE$ (slope of $BE$ is $\frac14$), so slope of $AC=-4$: $\frac{2b+t}{b-t}=-4$.
$2b+t=4t-4b\Rightarrow 6b=3t\Rightarrow b=\frac t2$.
Hence $B\left(-\frac{2t}{3},-\frac t6\right)$ and $C\left(\frac t2,t\right)$.
Centroid $G(h,k)=\left(\frac{t-\frac{2t}{3}+\frac t2}{3},\frac{-t-\frac t6+t}{3}\right)=\left(\frac{5t}{18},-\frac{t}{18}\right)$.
From $h=\frac{5t}{18}$ and $k=-\frac{t}{18}$: $t=\frac{18h}{5}$ and $t=-18k$, so $h+5k=0$.
Hence the locus of $G$ is the straight line $x+5y=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The altitudes meet at the origin $H$; with $H$ as origin the orthocentre property gives $\vec A\cdot\vec B=\vec B\cdot\vec C=\vec C\cdot\vec A$.
solution: The three altitudes $x+y=0$, $x-4y=0$, $2x-y=0$ all pass through $(0,0)$, so $H=O$.
With $H$ at the origin, $HA\perp BC$ etc. give $\vec A\cdot(\vec B-\vec C)=0$, $\vec B\cdot(\vec C-\vec A)=0$, i.e. $\vec A\cdot\vec B=\vec A\cdot\vec C=\vec B\cdot\vec C$.
Take $A=(t,-t)$, $B=(4\beta,\beta)$, $C=(c,2c)$: $\vec A\cdot\vec B=3t\beta$, $\vec A\cdot\vec C=-tc$, $\vec B\cdot\vec C=6\beta c$.
$3t\beta=-tc\Rightarrow c=-3\beta$; $6\beta c=-tc\Rightarrow\beta=-\frac t6$ (for $c\ne0$). So $B=\left(-\frac{2t}3,-\frac t6\right)$, $C=\left(\frac t2,t\right)$.
Centroid $\frac{A+B+C}{3}=\left(\frac{5t}{18},-\frac{t}{18}\right)$, which lies on $x+5y=0$ for every $t$ (matches).

useful_results: With the orthocentre at the origin, $\vec A\cdot\vec B=\vec B\cdot\vec C=\vec C\cdot\vec A$.
If the three altitude lines are fixed, every admissible triangle is a scaled copy about $H$ (the parameter $t$ is the scale), so the centroid, circumcentre etc. all move on lines through $H$.
Each vertex of a triangle lies on one altitude and its opposite side is $\perp$ to that altitude: use slopes $m_1m_2=-1$ to write two linear equations for two unknown vertices.

concepts: Pair of straight lines: lines through the origin at a given distance from a point
questions.question: The distance of a point $(x_1,y_1)$ from each of two straight lines which pass through the origin of coordinates is $\delta$. Find the combined equation of these straight lines.
questions.key_idea: Both lines $y=mx$ satisfy $\frac{|mx_1-y_1|}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}=\delta$, which is a quadratic in $m$; replacing $m$ by $\frac yx$ gives the pair.
solution: (Product of the distances of $P(x_1,y_1)$ from a pair $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$ is $\frac{|ax_1^2+2hx_1y_1+by_1^2|}{\sqrt{(a-b)^2+4h^2}}$; setting it equal to $\delta^2$ alone does not fix $a,h,b$, so we use slopes instead.)
Let the lines be $y=m_1x$ and $y=m_2x$. The distance of $(x_1,y_1)$ from $y=mx$ is $\delta=\frac{|mx_1-y_1|}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}$ for both $m_1$ and $m_2$.
Hence $m$ satisfies $\left(x_1^2-\delta^2\right)m^2-2x_1y_1\,m+\left(y_1^2-\delta^2\right)=0$, and $m_1,m_2$ are its two roots.
Put $m=\frac yx$: $\left(x_1^2-\delta^2\right)\frac{y^2}{x^2}-2x_1y_1\frac yx+\left(y_1^2-\delta^2\right)=0$.
Multiply by $x^2$: $\left(y_1^2-\delta^2\right)x^2-2x_1y_1\,xy+\left(x_1^2-\delta^2\right)y^2=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line has a misprint: it ends with $\left(x_1^2-\delta^2\right)xy^2$ whereas the correct term is $\left(x_1^2-\delta^2\right)y^2$ (the key is right). Its first two lines (the product-of-distances formula) are not used further, so they are mentioned only as a remark.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two lines through $O$ at distance $\delta$ from $P$ are the tangents from $O$ to the circle with centre $P$ and radius $\delta$; use $SS_1=T^2$.
solution: Circle with centre $P(x_1,y_1)$, radius $\delta$: $S\equiv x^2+y^2-2x_1x-2y_1y+k=0$ with $k=x_1^2+y_1^2-\delta^2$.
A line through $O$ is at distance $\delta$ from $P$ iff it touches this circle, so the pair is the pair of tangents from $O(0,0)$.
For the origin, $S_1=k$ and $T=-x_1x-y_1y+k$; the pair of tangents is $SS_1=T^2$.
$k\left(x^2+y^2-2x_1x-2y_1y+k\right)=\left(k-x_1x-y_1y\right)^2$.
Cancel $k^2$ and the linear terms: $(k-x_1^2)x^2+(k-y_1^2)y^2-2x_1y_1xy=0$.
With $k-x_1^2=y_1^2-\delta^2$ and $k-y_1^2=x_1^2-\delta^2$ this is $(y_1^2-\delta^2)x^2-2x_1y_1xy+(x_1^2-\delta^2)y^2=0$ (matches).

useful_results: Lines at a fixed distance $\delta$ from a fixed point $P$ are tangents to the circle (centre $P$, radius $\delta$): pair of tangents from a point is $SS_1=T^2$.
The pair is real iff $x_1^2+y_1^2>\delta^2$ (discriminant $4\delta^2(x_1^2+y_1^2-\delta^2)\ge0$).
Check: $P(2,0)$, $\delta=1$ gives $-x^2+3y^2=0$, i.e. $y=\pm\frac{x}{\sqrt3}$, and the distance from $(2,0)$ to $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt3}$ is $\frac{2/\sqrt3}{\sqrt{4/3}}=1$.

concepts: Pair of straight lines (factorisation); position of the origin inside a triangle and slope range of a variable line
questions.question: The sides of a triangle have the combined equation $x^2-3y^2-2xy+8y-4=0$. The third side, which is variable, always passes through the point $(-5,-1)$. If the range of values of the slope of the third line so that the origin is an interior point of the triangle lies in the interval $(a,b)$, then find $\left(a+\frac1{b^2}\right)$.
questions.key_idea: Factorise the pair, then notice $(-5,-1)$ lies on one of the two lines, so the triangle exists only for slopes in a range, and the origin must be on the vertex side of the third line.
solution: $x^2-2xy-3y^2=x^2-3xy+xy-3y^2=(x+y)(x-3y)$, so write the pair as $(x+y+c_1)(x-3y+c_2)=0$.
Compare the coefficients of $x$ and $y$: $c_1+c_2=0$ and $-3c_1+c_2=8$; subtracting, $4c_1=-8$.
So $c_1=-2$, $c_2=2$, and $c_1c_2=-4$ agrees with the constant term.
The two lines are $L_1:\ x+y-2=0$ and $L_2:\ x-3y+2=0$; they meet at the vertex $(1,1)$.
The point $(-5,-1)$ lies on $L_2$ ($-5+3+2=0$), so the variable line $y+1=m(x+5)$ cuts $L_1$ to complete the triangle.

The variable line is $y=mx+(5m-1)$. For $m<\frac13$ the vertex $(1,1)$ lies above it, so the triangle lies above the third side; the origin is inside only if it is also above the line, i.e. the $y$-intercept is negative: $5m-1<0\Rightarrow m<\frac15$.
A triangle is formed only if the variable line is not parallel to $L_1$ (slope $-1$) and cuts $L_1$ on the correct ray, i.e. $m>-1$ (and $m\neq\frac13$ since that is $L_2$ itself).
So $m\in\left(-1,\frac15\right)$: $a=-1$, $b=\frac15$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last line reads 'a+b = 4', but the question asks for $a+\frac1{b^2}=-1+25=24$ (the key 24 is right). Also '$5m-1=0\Rightarrow m<\frac15$' should read $5m-1<0\Rightarrow m<\frac15$, and the reason for $m>-1$ (slope $-1$ is parallel to $L_1$, so no triangle) has been written out.

alternate_solutions.idea: Barycentric coordinates: write the origin as a positive combination of the three vertices and read off the range of the vertex on $L_1$.
solution: Vertices: $V=(1,1)$, $W=(-5,-1)$ and $D=(d,2-d)$ on $L_1$; $D$ must lie on the ray of $L_1$ with $d>1$ (the ray bounding the wedge that contains the origin).

Solve $O=\lambda V+\mu W+
u D$, $\lambda+\mu+
u=1$. From the $x$ and $y$ equations: $\lambda-5\mu+d
u=0$ and $\lambda-\mu+(2-d)
u=0$.

Subtract: $-4\mu+(2d-2)
u=0$, so $\mu= rac{d-1}{2}
u$; the sum equation then gives $
u= rac1{2(d-1)}$, $\mu= rac14$, $\lambda= rac{3d-5}{4(d-1)}$.
The origin is inside iff $\lambda,\mu,\nu>0$: $d>1$ and $3d-5>0$, i.e. $d>\frac53$.
Slope of the line through $W$ and $D$: $m=\frac{(2-d)+1}{d+5}=\frac{3-d}{d+5}$, which decreases from $\frac15$ (at $d=\frac53$) towards $-1$ (as $d\to\infty$).
So $m\in\left(-1,\frac15\right)$ and $a+\frac1{b^2}=-1+25=24$ (matches).

useful_results: Factorise a pair $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ as $(l_1x+m_1y+c_1)(l_2x+m_2y+c_2)$: the quadratic part fixes the directions, then solve two linear equations for $c_1,c_2$ and check $c_1c_2$ against $c$.

A point is inside a triangle iff it is on the same side as the opposite vertex for every side; the extremes of the slope range correspond to the variable line becoming parallel to a side, passing through a vertex, or through the point itself ($m=\frac15$ passes through the origin).
Barycentric coordinates $(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ all positive $\iff$ point strictly inside; here $\mu=\frac14$ stays constant because the origin lies on a fixed cevian direction.

concepts: Pair of straight lines forming a triangle: angles, area and inradius
questions.question:
Consider a line pair $2x^2+3xy-2y^2-10x+15y-28=0$ and another line $L$ passing through the origin with gradient $3$. The line pair and the line $L$ form a triangle whose vertices are $A$, $B$ and $C$.
(a) Find the sum of the cotangents of the interior angles of the triangle $ABC$.
(b) Find the area of the triangle $ABC$.
(c) Find the radius of the circle touching all the three sides of the triangle.
questions.key_idea: The slopes of the pair come from $2m^2-3m-2=0$; the two lines of the pair are perpendicular, so the triangle is right-angled.
solution: The pair is $2x^2+3xy-2y^2-10x+15y-28=0$ and $L:\ y=3x$. The homogeneous part $2x^2+3xy-2y^2=0$ gives the slopes of the pair: with $m=\frac yx$, $2+3m-2m^2=0$.
$2m^2-3m-2=0\Rightarrow 2m^2-4m+m-2=0\Rightarrow(2m+1)(m-2)=0$, so $m=-\frac12$ or $m=2$.
Slopes of the three sides: $m_1=3$ (line $L$), $m_2=2$, $m_3=-\frac12$.
$\tan II=\frac{m_2-m_3}{1+m_2m_3}=\frac{2+\frac12}{1-1}=\infty$, so this angle is $90^\circ$ (the two lines of the pair are perpendicular).
$\tan III=\left|\frac{m_3-m_1}{1+m_1m_3}\right|=\left|\frac{-\frac12-3}{1-\frac32}\right|=7$.
For the vertices, factorise the pair: $2x^2+3xy-2y^2=(x+2y)(2x-y)$, so write it as $(x+2y+C_1)(2x-y+C_2)=0$.
Points of intersection: $A\left(-\frac15,\frac{18}5\right)$ (of the pair), $B(4,12)$ ($y=3x$ with $2x-y+4=0$), $C(1,3)$ ($y=3x$ with $x+2y-7=0$).

(b) $\Delta ABC=\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}-\frac15&\frac{18}5&1\\4&12&1\\1&3&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac1{10}\left|\begin{matrix}-6&3&5\\3&9&1\\0&0&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac1{10}\,|-54-9|=\frac{63}{10}$.
(c) Sides: $AB=\frac{21}{\sqrt5}$, $AC=\frac{3}{\sqrt5}$, $BC=3\sqrt{10}$; the triangle is right-angled at $A$, so $r=\frac{AB+AC-BC}{2}$.
$r=\frac12\left(\frac{24}{\sqrt5}-3\sqrt{10}\right)=\frac{12\sqrt5}{5}-\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}=\frac{3}{10}\left(8\sqrt5-5\sqrt{10}\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's $\tan III$ line is garbled ($\frac{-17}{1+1}$); the correct value is $\tan III=7$ (consistent with the $\frac17$ it later uses for $\cot III$). The factorisation part is labelled '(d)' instead of continuing the working for (b). Part (c) (inradius) has no working in the PDF: it was written here using the right angle at $A$, giving $\frac{3}{10}(8\sqrt5-5\sqrt{10})$, the printed key.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot the right angle at $A$ (slopes $-\frac12$ and $2$); the legs are then perpendicular distances, and $\cot B+\cot C=\frac{AB}{AC}+\frac{AC}{AB}$.
solution: The lines $x+2y-7=0$ and $2x-y+4=0$ are perpendicular (coefficient sum $2-2=0$ in the pair), so $\angle A=90^\circ$ and $\cot A=0$.
At $B$ the angle between $y=3x$ and slope $2$ has $\tan B=\frac{1}{7}=\frac{AC}{AB}$, so $\cot B+\cot C=\frac{AB}{AC}+\frac{AC}{AB}=7+\frac17=\frac{50}{7}$.
Leg $AC$ = distance of $C(1,3)$ from $2x-y+4=0$: $\frac{|2-3+4|}{\sqrt5}=\frac3{\sqrt5}$. Leg $AB$ = distance of $B(4,12)$ from $x+2y-7=0$: $\frac{|4+24-7|}{\sqrt5}=\frac{21}{\sqrt5}$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot\frac{3}{\sqrt5}\cdot\frac{21}{\sqrt5}=\frac{63}{10}$.
Hypotenuse $BC=\sqrt{(4-1)^2+(12-3)^2}=3\sqrt{10}$, and $r=\frac{AB+AC-BC}{2}=\frac{3}{10}(8\sqrt5-5\sqrt{10})\approx0.62$ (matches).

useful_results: A pair $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+\dots=0$ is a pair of perpendicular lines iff $a+b=0$ (here $2-2=0$): the triangle is right-angled and areas/inradius become leg computations.
In any triangle $\cot A+\cot B+\cot C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{4\Delta}$; check: $\frac{90+88.2+1.8}{4(6.3)}=\frac{180}{25.2}=\frac{50}7$.
Right triangle: $r=\frac{\text{leg}_1+\text{leg}_2-\text{hyp}}{2}$; angle between lines $\tan\phi=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$ ($\infty$ when $m_1m_2=-1$).

concepts: Pair of straight lines: parallelogram formed by two line pairs (area and diagonals)
questions.question: The two line pairs $y^2-4y+3=0$ and $x^2+4xy+4y^2-5x-10y+4=0$ enclose a four-sided convex polygon. Find (i) the area of the polygon and (ii) the lengths of its diagonals.
questions.key_idea: Both pairs factorise into parallel lines, so the polygon is a parallelogram whose vertices are found by intersecting the lines.
solution: $y^2-4y+3=0\Rightarrow y=3,\ y=1$.
The lines are $y=1$, $y=3$, $x+2y=1$ and $x+2y=4$.
(i) Area by the determinant (vertices in order $A,D,C,B$): $\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}-1&2&-2&-5&-1\\1&1&3&3&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac12\left[-1-2+6+2-6+15-5+3\right]=6$.
(ii) Diagonal $AC=\sqrt{(-1+2)^2+(1-3)^2}=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Two pairs of parallel lines form a parallelogram: with side vectors $\vec u,\vec v$, area $=|\vec u\times\vec v|$ and the diagonals are $|\vec u\pm\vec v|$.
solution: From $A(-1,1)$ the sides are $\vec u=\overrightarrow{AD}=(3,0)$ (along $y=1$, between $x+2y=1$ and $x+2y=4$) and $\vec v=\overrightarrow{AB}=(-4,2)$ (along $x+2y=1$, between $y=1$ and $y=3$).
Area $=|\vec u\times\vec v|=|3\cdot2-0\cdot(-4)|=6$.
Diagonals: $\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec u+\vec v=(-1,2)$, length $\sqrt5$; $\overrightarrow{DB}=\vec v-\vec u=(-7,2)$, length $\sqrt{53}$.

useful_results: Area enclosed by $a_1x+b_1y=p,\ p'$ and $a_2x+b_2y=q,\ q'$ is $\dfrac{|p-p'|\,|q-q'|}{|a_1b_2-a_2b_1|}$; here $\frac{3\cdot2}{|1\cdot1-0\cdot2|}=6$.
Parallelogram law: $d_1^2+d_2^2=2(a^2+b^2)$; diagonals are $|\vec u+\vec v|$ and $|\vec u-\vec v|$.
A quadratic equation that is a perfect square plus linear terms in $(x+2y)$ factorises as a quadratic in that single combination.

concepts: Pair of straight lines: parallelogram with diagonals meeting at the origin
questions.question: Find the equation of the two straight lines which, together with those given by the equation $6x^2-xy-y^2+x+12y-35=0$, will make a parallelogram whose diagonals intersect at the origin.
questions.key_idea: The opposite vertex of the pair's intersection point is its reflection in the origin, and the new lines are parallel to the given ones through that vertex.
solution: The vertex $A$ is the intersection of $2x-y+5=0$ and $3x+y-7=0$: adding gives $5x=2$, so $A\left(\frac25,\frac{29}5\right)$.
The diagonals meet at the origin (their common midpoint), so the opposite vertex is $C\left(-\frac25,-\frac{29}5\right)$.
The other two sides pass through $C$ and are parallel to the given ones: $2x-y+K_1=0$ and $3x+y+K_2=0$.
Through $C$: $-\frac45+\frac{29}{5}+K_1=0\Rightarrow K_1=-5$; and $-\frac65-\frac{29}5+K_2=0\Rightarrow K_2=7$.
Combined equation: $(2x-y-5)(3x+y+7)=0$, i.e. $6x^2-xy-y^2-x-12y-35=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A parallelogram is symmetric about its centre, so the missing pair is the half-turn image of the given pair: replace $(x,y)$ by $(-x,-y)$.
solution: The half-turn about the centre $O$ maps each side of the parallelogram to the opposite side.
So the required pair is the image of the given pair under $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$.
In $6x^2-xy-y^2+x+12y-35=0$ the terms of degree $2$ and the constant are unchanged, the linear terms change sign.
Hence the required pair is $6x^2-xy-y^2-x-12y-35=0$ (matches), which factorises as $(2x-y-5)(3x+y+7)$.

useful_results: Point reflection in $(p,q)$: $(x,y)\to(2p-x,2q-y)$; in the origin it only flips the sign of the linear terms of a conic or pair of lines.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are images under the half-turn about its centre; parallel sides share the same homogeneous part, so the new pair has the same $ax^2+2hxy+by^2$.
Check: the vertex $C$ of the new pair is $(-\frac25,-\frac{29}5)=-A$.

concepts: Straight line through the origin meeting given lines (distances along a line)
Bounds on trigonometric expressions (maximum value)
questions.question:
A straight line passing through $O(0,0)$ cuts the lines $x=a$, $y=b$ and $x+y=8$ at $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively such that $OA\cdot OB\cdot OC=48\sqrt2$ and $f(a,b)\le0$, where $f(x,y)=\left| rac yx- rac32ight|+(3x-2y)^6+\sqrt{ex+2y-2e-6}$.
(i) Find the point of intersection of the lines $x=a$ and $y=b$.
(ii) Find the value of $(OA+OB+OC)$.
(iii) Find the equation of the line $OA$.
questions.key_idea: A sum of non-negative terms that is $\le0$ forces every term to be $0$; later $\sin2\theta(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)=\sqrt2$ is attained only at its maximum.
solution: (i) Each term of $f$ is non-negative, so $f(a,b)\le0$ forces $f(a,b)=0$ and every term zero.
$\left|\frac ba-\frac32\right|=0\Rightarrow 2b=3a$ (the term $(3a-2b)^6=0$ gives the same relation).
$\sqrt{ea+2b-2e-6}=0\Rightarrow ea+2b-2e-6=0$; with $b=\frac{3a}{2}$ this is $(e+3)(a-2)=0$, so $a=2$ and $b=3$.
The lines $x=2$ and $y=3$ meet at $(2,3)$.
(ii) Let the line $OA$ make angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis: $A=(r_1\cos\theta,r_1\sin\theta)$ on $x=2$ gives $r_1\cos\theta=2$.
$B=(r_2\cos\theta,r_2\sin\theta)$ on $y=3$ gives $r_2\sin\theta=3$.
$C=(r_3\cos\theta,r_3\sin\theta)$ on $x+y=8$ gives $r_3=\frac{8}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}$.
$r_1r_2r_3=48\sqrt2\Rightarrow\frac{2\cdot3\cdot8}{\cos\theta\sin\theta(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}=48\sqrt2\Rightarrow\sin\theta\cos\theta(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt2}$.

So $\sin2\theta\,(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)=\sqrt2$. Since $\sin2\theta\le1$ and $\sin\theta+\cos\theta\le\sqrt2$, equality needs $\sin2\theta=1$ and $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2$, i.e. $\theta=45^\circ$.
$r_1=2\sqrt2$, $r_2=3\sqrt2$, $r_3=\frac{8}{\sqrt2}=4\sqrt2$, so $OA+OB+OC=9\sqrt2$.
(iii) $m=\tan45^\circ=1$ and the line passes through $O(0,0)$: $y=x$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the radicand condition as 'ea+2b-ea-6=0', a misprint for $ea+2b-2e-6=0$ (the printed radicand is $ex+2y-2e-6$). The solution $(a,b)=(2,3)$ is correct. The PDF also asserts '$\theta=45^\circ$' without the reason (maximum values), which has been added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with the slope $m$ of $OA$ instead of an angle: the condition becomes a polynomial equation with a double root at $m=1$.
solution: Let $OA$ be $y=mx$. Then $A=(2,2m)$, $B=\left(\frac3m,3\right)$, $C=\left(\frac8{1+m},\frac{8m}{1+m}\right)$ with the common factor $\sqrt{1+m^2}$: $OA=2\sqrt{1+m^2}$, $OB=\frac{3\sqrt{1+m^2}}{|m|}$, $OC=\frac{8\sqrt{1+m^2}}{|1+m|}$.
$OA\cdot OB\cdot OC=\frac{48(1+m^2)^{3/2}}{|m||1+m|}=48\sqrt2\Rightarrow(1+m^2)^3=2m^2(1+m)^2$.
Expand: $m^6+m^4-4m^3+m^2+1=0$, which factorises as $(m-1)^2\left(m^4+2m^3+4m^2+2m+1\right)=0$.
The quartic factor equals $(m^2+m)^2+3m^2+2m+1>0$ (since $3m^2+2m+1$ has negative discriminant), so $m=1$ only.
Hence $y=x$, $OA=2\sqrt2$, $OB=3\sqrt2$, $OC=4\sqrt2$ and the sum is $9\sqrt2$ (matches).

useful_results: If every term of a sum is $\ge0$ (even powers, modulus, square root) and the sum is $\le0$, each term vanishes: this solves 'f(a,b)\le0' type conditions in one line.
For a line through the origin at angle $\theta$, its distances to $x=p$, $y=q$, $x+y=s$ are $\frac{p}{\cos\theta}$, $\frac q{\sin\theta}$, $\frac{s}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}$ (signed along the line).
$\sin2\theta\,(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)\le\sqrt2$ with equality only at $\theta=\frac\pi4$: an equation hitting the maximum of a product of bounded factors has a unique solution.

concepts: Angle between two lines and medians of a right-angled triangle
questions.question: The triangle $ABC$, right-angled at $C$, has medians $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$. $AD$ lies along the line $y=x+3$ and $BE$ lies along the line $y=2x+4$. If the length of the hypotenuse is $60$, find the area of the triangle $ABC$.
questions.key_idea: The acute angle between the two leg-medians is given by the slopes ($\tan\theta=\frac13$) and also by the legs, giving $ab$.
solution: Let $CA=b$, $CB=a$. Since the angle at $C$ is $90^\circ$ and the hypotenuse is $60$: $a^2+b^2=60^2$.
The angle $\theta$ between the medians (lines of slopes $1$ and $2$): $\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\left|\frac{1-2}{1+2}\right|=\frac13$.
In $\triangle CBE$ (right-angled at $C$, $CE=\frac b2$), let $\alpha=\angle CBE$: $\tan\alpha=\frac{CE}{BC}=\frac{b/2}{a}=\frac{b}{2a}$.
In $\triangle ADC$ (right-angled at $C$, $CD=\frac a2$): $\tan\angle ADC=\frac{AC}{CD}=\frac{b}{a/2}=\frac{2b}{a}$.
$\angle ADC$ is the exterior angle of $\triangle GDB$ ($G$ the centroid) so $\angle ADC=\theta+\alpha$ and $\tan(\theta+\alpha)=\frac{2b}{a}$.
$\frac{\tan\theta+\tan\alpha}{1-\tan\theta\tan\alpha}=\frac{2b}{a}\Rightarrow\frac{\frac13+\frac{b}{2a}}{1-\frac13\cdot\frac b{2a}}=\frac{2b}{a}$.
Simplify: $\frac{2a+3b}{6a-b}=\frac{2b}{a}\Rightarrow 2a^2+3ab=12ab-2b^2\Rightarrow 2(a^2+b^2)=9ab$.
Area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12ab=400$ sq. units.
questions.correction_note: In the PDF the step 'In $\triangle CBE$: $\tan\theta=\frac{CE}{BC}=\frac b{2a}$' is mislabelled: that ratio is $\tan\alpha$ ($\alpha=\angle CBE$), while $\tan\theta=\frac13$ comes from the slopes; the next line 'tan(θ+α)=tanθ+tab α...' is a typing slip. The corrected labels give the same $ab=800$ and area $400$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $ABG$ ($G$ the centroid): its area is $\frac{\Delta}3$ and the law of cosines on $AB$ gives $\tan\theta=\frac{3\Delta}{c^2}$ directly, so $\Delta=\frac{c^2\tan\theta}{3}$.
solution: Let $GA$, $GB$ be the centroid-to-vertex distances and $\theta$ the acute angle between the medians; $\angle AGB=180^\circ-\theta$ and $[ABG]=\frac\Delta3$.
Medians to the legs ($C=90^\circ$): $m_a^2=b^2+\frac{a^2}4$, $m_b^2=a^2+\frac{b^2}4$, so $GA^2+GB^2=\frac49(m_a^2+m_b^2)=\frac49\cdot\frac54(a^2+b^2)=\frac59c^2$.
Law of cosines in $\triangle AGB$: $c^2=GA^2+GB^2+2\,GA\cdot GB\cos\theta\Rightarrow GA\cdot GB\cos\theta=\frac{2c^2}{9}$.
Area: $\frac12GA\cdot GB\sin\theta=\frac\Delta3\Rightarrow GA\cdot GB\sin\theta=\frac{2\Delta}{3}$.
Divide: $\tan\theta=\frac{2\Delta/3}{2c^2/9}=\frac{3\Delta}{c^2}$. With $\tan\theta=\frac13$ and $c=60$: $\Delta=\frac{c^2}{9}=400$ (matches).

useful_results: In a right triangle (right angle at $C$, hypotenuse $c$), the acute angle $\theta$ between the medians to the legs satisfies $\tan\theta=\dfrac{3ab}{2(a^2+b^2)}=\dfrac{3\Delta}{c^2}$.
Hence $\tan\theta\le\frac34$ (equality for the isosceles right triangle), and $\Delta=\dfrac{c^2\tan\theta}{3}$: here $\tan\theta=\frac13$ gives $\frac{3600}{9}=400$.
$m_a^2+m_b^2=\frac54c^2$ for the medians to the legs of a right triangle; the centroid divides each median $2:1$.

concepts: Locus of the intersection of two variable lines (elimination of a parameter)
questions.question: A straight line $L$ through the origin meets the lines $x+y=1$ and $x+y=3$ at $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Through $P$ and $Q$ two straight lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ are drawn, parallel to $2x-y=5$ and $3x+y=5$ respectively. Lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect at $R$. Show that the locus of $R$, as $L$ varies, is a straight line.
questions.key_idea: Writing $L_1$ and $L_2$ with the same parameter $\frac1{m+1}$ on the right means a suitable ratio of the two equations eliminates $m$ linearly.
solution: Let $L$ be $y=mx$. It meets $x+y=1$ at $P\left(\frac1{m+1},\frac m{m+1}\right)$ and $x+y=3$ at $Q\left(\frac3{m+1},\frac{3m}{m+1}\right)$.
$L_1$ through $P$ with slope $2$: $y-\frac{m}{m+1}=2\left(x-\frac1{m+1}\right)\Rightarrow y-2x-1=-\frac{3}{m+1}$ (1).
$L_2$ through $Q$ with slope $-3$: $y-\frac{3m}{m+1}=-3\left(x-\frac{3}{m+1}\right)\Rightarrow y+3x-3=\frac{6}{m+1}$ (2).
Dividing (1) by (2): $\frac{y-2x-1}{y+3x-3}=-\frac12$.
$2y-4x-2=-y-3x+3\Rightarrow x-3y+5=0$, which is a straight line.

alternate_solutions.idea: Because $x+y=1$ and $x+y=3$ are parallel, the homothety about $O$ gives $Q=3P$; then $R$ is found with vectors and two parameters.
solution: $P$ and $Q$ lie on one line through $O$ and on parallel lines $x+y=1$, $x+y=3$, so $\vec Q=3\vec P$ with $P=(p,1-p)$.
$L_1$ has direction $(1,2)$, $L_2$ has direction $(1,-3)$; $R=P+s(1,2)=3P+t(1,-3)$.
So $s(1,2)-t(1,-3)=2P=(2p,2-2p)$; adding the components: $3s+2t=2$ (using $p+(1-p)=1$).
$R=P+s(1,2)=\left(\frac{3s-t}{2},\frac{6s+3t}{2}\right)$ (substituting $p=\frac{s-t}{2}$).

useful_results: If two moving lines can be written $\ell_1(x,y)=\alpha\,g(m)$ and $\ell_2(x,y)=\beta\,g(m)$ with the same function $g(m)$ (here $g=\frac1{m+1}$), then $\ell_1:\ell_2=\alpha:\beta$ is free of $m$ and the locus is a straight line.
Points of a line through $O$ on parallel lines $x+y=c_1$, $x+y=c_2$ are in the ratio $c_1:c_2$ from $O$ (here $Q=3P$).

concepts: Intercepts of a line through a fixed point
AM–GM inequality (minimum value)
questions.question: A straight line $L$ with negative slope passes through the point $(8,2)$ and cuts the positive coordinate axes at the points $P$ and $Q$. Find the absolute minimum value of $OP+OQ$, as $L$ varies, where $O$ is the origin.
questions.key_idea: $OP+OQ=10+\frac{2}{|m|}+8|m|$ is a sum of two reciprocal-type terms, so AM–GM gives the minimum.
solution: The line is $y-2=m(x-8)$ with $m<0$.
Its intercepts: $P\left(8-\frac2m,\,0\right)$ and $Q(0,\,2-8m)$, both positive since $m<0$.
$OP+OQ=\left|8-\frac2m\right|+|2-8m|=10+\frac{2}{(-m)}+8(-m)$.
Equality holds when $\frac2{(-m)}=8(-m)$, i.e. $m=-\frac12$ (then $P=(12,0)$, $Q=(0,6)$), so the minimum is attained and equals $18$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working ends with a leftover line 'Area of $\triangle OPQ$ is minimum when $(8,2)$ is the midpoint... $=32$', which answers a different question (minimum area). It is not part of this question and has been dropped; the AM–GM working and the answer $18$ are correct. The attainment of equality ($m=-\frac12$) has been added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Intercept form $\frac xp+\frac yq=1$ with $\frac8p+\frac2q=1$, and Cauchy–Schwarz on $(p+q)\left(\frac8p+\frac2q\right)$.
solution: Let $P=(p,0)$, $Q=(0,q)$ with $p,q>0$; the line $\frac xp+\frac yq=1$ passes through $(8,2)$, so $\frac8p+\frac2q=1$.
$p+q=(p+q)\left(\frac8p+\frac2q\right)$.
By Cauchy–Schwarz, $(p+q)\left(\frac8p+\frac2q\right)\ge\left(\sqrt8+\sqrt2\right)^2=\left(3\sqrt2\right)^2=18$.
Equality when $\frac pq=\frac{\sqrt8}{\sqrt2}=2$: with $\frac8p+\frac2q=1$ this gives $p=12$, $q=6$ (slope $-\frac12<0$).
So the minimum of $OP+OQ$ is $18$ (matches).

useful_results: For a line through $(a,b)$ with positive intercepts $p,q$: $\min(p+q)=(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^2$, attained at $p=a+\sqrt{ab}$, $q=b+\sqrt{ab}$ (here $18$ at $p=12,q=6$).
For the same family: minimum area of $\triangle OPQ=2ab$ (when $(a,b)$ is the midpoint of $PQ$): $32$ for $(8,2)$; minimum length of $PQ$ is $\left(a^{2/3}+b^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}\approx13.2$.
AM–GM on terms of the form $\frac{c}{t}+dt$ ($c,d,t>0$) gives $\ge2\sqrt{cd}$, equality at $t=\sqrt{c/d}$.

concepts: Area of a quadrilateral in coordinates; maximum of a quadratic function
questions.paragraph: Let $ABCD$ be a square with sides of unit length. Points $E$ and $F$ are taken on sides $AB$ and $AD$ respectively so that $AE=AF$. Let $P$ be a point inside the square $ABCD$.
questions.question: The maximum possible area of quadrilateral $CDFE$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put $AE=AF=x$; the area is a quadratic in $x$ whose vertex lies inside $(0,1)$.
solution: Area of $CDFE$ by the determinant (vertices $E,F,D,C$): $\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}x&0&0&1&x\\0&x&1&1&0\end{matrix}\right|=\frac12\left|x^2-1-x\right|$.
$A=\frac12\left|x^2-x-1\right|=\frac12\left(1+x-x^2\right)$ for $x\in(0,1)$ (since $x^2-x-1<0$ there).
The quadratic $x^2-x-1$ has its vertex at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac12\in(0,1)$.
Vertex value: $-\frac{D}{4a}=-\frac{1+4}{4}=-\frac54$, so $A_{\max}=\frac12\cdot\frac54=\frac58$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract the two cut-off right triangles from the unit square and complete the square.
solution: With $AE=AF=x$: $[AEF]=\frac{x^2}2$ and $[EBC]=\frac12(1-x)\cdot1$.
Complete the square: $\frac{1+x-x^2}{2}=\frac58-\frac12\left(x-\frac12\right)^2\le\frac58$.
Equality at $x=\frac12$, so the maximum area is $\frac58$ (option C) (matches).

useful_results: Area of a polygon from vertices in order: $\frac12\left|\sum(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)\right|$ (shoelace); for shapes inside a square it is often quicker to subtract corner triangles from the square.
$ax^2+bx+c$ with $a<0$ has maximum $c-\frac{b^2}{4a}$ at $x=-\frac b{2a}$; check that the vertex lies in the allowed interval.
Here $x=0$ gives area $\frac12$ and $x=1$ gives $\frac12$, so the maximum $\frac58$ lies strictly between.

concepts: Distance formula; coordinates of a square
questions.paragraph: Let $ABCD$ be a square with sides of unit length. Points $E$ and $F$ are taken on sides $AB$ and $AD$ respectively so that $AE=AF$. Let $P$ be a point inside the square $ABCD$.
questions.question: The value of $(PA)^2-(PB)^2+(PC)^2-(PD)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Take $P=(\alpha,\beta)$ and expand: all terms cancel in pairs.
solution: $Z=\alpha^2+\beta^2-(\alpha-1)^2-\beta^2+(\alpha-1)^2+(\beta-1)^2-\alpha^2-(\beta-1)^2$.
Terms cancel in pairs: $\alpha^2$ with $-\alpha^2$, $\beta^2$ with $-\beta^2$, $(\alpha-1)^2$ with $-(\alpha-1)^2$ and $(\beta-1)^2$ with $-(\beta-1)^2$, so $Z=0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expression for $Z$ contains misprints: it prints $(\beta+2)^2$ and $(\beta\alpha)^2$ where $(\beta-1)^2$ and $\alpha^2+(\beta-1)^2$ are meant, i.e. $PC^2$ and $PD^2$ are mis-typed. With the correct distances the sum is $0$, as the key says.

alternate_solutions.idea: British Flag Theorem: for a rectangle $ABCD$ and any point $P$, $PA^2+PC^2=PB^2+PD^2$.
solution: Let $O$ be the centre of the rectangle, with $\vec{OA}=-\vec{OC}=\vec u$ and $\vec{OB}=-\vec{OD}=\vec v$, $|\vec u|=|\vec v|$ (diagonals of a rectangle are equal).
For any $P$: $PA^2+PC^2=|\vec p-\vec u|^2+|\vec p+\vec u|^2=2|\vec p|^2+2|\vec u|^2$.
Likewise $PB^2+PD^2=2|\vec p|^2+2|\vec v|^2$.
Since $|\vec u|=|\vec v|$, $PA^2+PC^2=PB^2+PD^2$, so $PA^2-PB^2+PC^2-PD^2=0$ (matches).

useful_results: British Flag Theorem: for any point $P$ in the plane of a rectangle $ABCD$, $PA^2+PC^2=PB^2+PD^2$ (even if $P$ is outside).
For a general parallelogram $PA^2+PC^2-PB^2-PD^2=\frac{AC^2-BD^2}{2}$, a constant that is $0$ exactly when the diagonals are equal, i.e. for a rectangle.
Check with $P=A$: $0-1+2-1=0$.

concepts: Area of a triangle and distance formula (line dividing a square in a given ratio)
questions.paragraph: Let $ABCD$ be a square with sides of unit length. Points $E$ and $F$ are taken on sides $AB$ and $AD$ respectively so that $AE=AF$. Let $P$ be a point inside the square $ABCD$.
questions.question: Let a line passing through point $A$ divide the square $ABCD$ into two parts so that the area of one portion is double the other. Then the length of the portion of the line inside the square is:
questions.key_idea: The smaller part has area $\frac13$ and is a right triangle with legs $1$ and $x$, so $x=\frac23$.
solution: Take $A(0,0)$, $B(1,0)$, $C(1,1)$, $D(0,1)$; let the line through $A$ meet $BC$ at $(1,x)$.
One part is double the other, so the smaller part has area $\frac13$ of the square: $3\mathcal A=1$, $\mathcal A=\frac13$.
The smaller part is the triangle with legs $1$ and $x$: $\frac12\cdot1\cdot x=\frac13$.
So $x=\frac23$.
Length of the line inside the square $=\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sqrt{1+\frac49}=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3}$.
useful_results: A line from a vertex of a unit square cutting off area fraction $f\le\frac12$ meets the far side at height $2f$, so its length is $\sqrt{1+4f^2}$; here $f=\frac13$ gives $\frac{\sqrt{13}}3$.
The other possibility (the line meeting $CD$) is the mirror image in the diagonal $AC$ and has the same length.

Limits: $f\to0$ gives length $1$ (the side $AB$) and $f=\frac12$ gives $\sqrt2$ (the diagonal $AC$); the length $\sqrt{1+4f^2}$ increases with $f$, and $\frac{\sqrt{13}}{3}\approx1.20$ lies between them.

concepts: Equation of a line through a midpoint, intersection point and area of a triangle in coordinates
Range of a rational function of $\tan\theta$
questions.paragraph: The base of an isosceles triangle is equal to $4$, the base angle is equal to $45^\circ$. A straight line cuts the extension of the base at a point $M$ at the angle $\theta$ and bisects the lateral side of the triangle which is nearest to $M$.
questions.question: The area $A$ of the quadrilateral which the straight line cuts off from the given triangle is:
questions.key_idea: The quadrilateral is the triangle minus the small triangle $APQ$, whose area comes from the intersection point $Q$ of the line with $AC$.
solution: Take $B(0,0)$, $C(4,0)$, $A(2,2)$ (base $4$, base angles $45^\circ$, so the apex angle is $90^\circ$); $M$ lies on the extension of the base beyond $B$, so the line bisects $AB$ at $P(1,1)$.
Equation of the line $PM$: $y-1=\tan\theta\,(x-1)$.
$AC$ is $y=4-x$. Its intersection $Q$ with $PM$: $4-x-1=\tan\theta\,(x-1)\Rightarrow x=\frac{3+\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
So $Q\equiv\left(\frac{3+\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta},\frac{1+3\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}\right)$.
Area of $\triangle APQ=\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\2&2&1\\\frac{3+\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}&\frac{1+3\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
Area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12\cdot4\cdot2=4$.
The quadrilateral $PBCQ$ cut off has area $A=4-\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac{4+4\tan\theta-1+\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac{3+5\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$ (option D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's shared solution for Q21–Q23 stops after the area of $\triangle APQ$; the subtraction from the area $4$ of $\triangle ABC$ that gives the printed key (D) was added here.

alternate_solutions.idea: The apex angle is $90^\circ$, so $\triangle APQ$ is right-angled at $A$ and $AQ=AP\tan(45^\circ-\theta)$: no coordinates for $Q$ are needed.
solution: $\triangle ABC$ has base angles $45^\circ$, so $\angle A=90^\circ$; $AP=\frac12AB=\sqrt2$.
The line $PM$ makes angle $\theta$ with the base while $PA$ makes $45^\circ$, so $\angle APQ=45^\circ-\theta$.
In the right triangle $APQ$: $AQ=AP\tan(45^\circ-\theta)=\sqrt2\,\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
$[APQ]=\frac12\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2\,\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
$A=[ABC]-[APQ]=4-\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}=\frac{3+5\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$ (matches).

useful_results: An isosceles triangle with base angles $45^\circ$ is right-angled at the apex; a median-type cut from a midpoint of a leg gives areas via $\tan(45^\circ-\theta)=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
A cut-off area expressed as $\frac{\alpha+\beta t}{1+t}=\beta+\frac{\alpha-\beta}{1+t}$ is monotonic in $t=\tan\theta$: rewrite as a constant plus a Möbius term before ranging it.
Check at $\theta\to0$: the line is $y=1$, cutting off the trapezium of area $4-1=3$, and the formula gives $3$.

concepts: Range of a rational function of $\tan\theta$; limiting positions of a line
questions.paragraph: The base of an isosceles triangle is equal to $4$, the base angle is equal to $45^\circ$. A straight line cuts the extension of the base at a point $M$ at the angle $\theta$ and bisects the lateral side of the triangle which is nearest to $M$.
questions.question: The range of values of $A$, for different values of $\theta$, lies in the interval:
questions.key_idea: $\tan\theta$ is restricted to $(0,1)$, and $A=5-\frac2{1+\tan\theta}$ is increasing, so its range is between its end values.
solution: Take $B(0,0)$, $C(4,0)$, $A(2,2)$ (base $4$, base angles $45^\circ$, so the apex angle is $90^\circ$); $M$ lies on the extension of the base beyond $B$, so the line bisects $AB$ at $P(1,1)$.
The line through $P(1,1)$ with slope $t=\tan\theta$ meets the base line $y=0$ at $x=1-\frac1t$; this is to the left of $B$ (so $M$ is on the extension of the base) only if $0<t<1$.
For $0<t<1$ the point $Q$ lies on $AC$ itself (its $x$-coordinate $\frac{3+t}{1+t}$ decreases from $3$ to $2$), so $0<\theta<45^\circ$.
$A$ is an increasing function of $t$ on $(0,1)$.
As $t\to0^+$, $A\to5-2=3$; as $t\to1^-$, $A\to5-1=4$ (neither end is attained).
Hence $A\in(3,4)$ (option D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the two limiting positions of the line: parallel to the base ($\theta\to0$) and through the apex ($\theta\to45^\circ$).
solution: $A=[ABC]-[APQ]=4-[APQ]$ and $[APQ]\in(0,1)$ as $\theta$ runs over $(0,45^\circ)$.
$\theta\to0$: the line becomes $y=1$ and $\triangle APQ$ is the top triangle of height $1$ out of $2$, similar to $ABC$ with ratio $\frac12$: area $\frac14\cdot4=1$, so $A\to3$.
$\theta\to45^\circ$: the line passes through $A$, $Q\to A$ and $[APQ]\to0$, so $A\to4$.
$[APQ]=\frac{1-t}{1+t}$ is strictly decreasing from $1$ to $0$, so $A$ takes every value in $(3,4)$ (matches).

useful_results: To find the range of a monotonic expression, evaluate it at the two limiting positions of the geometric parameter; check monotonicity from the form const$\,\pm\,\frac{k}{1+t}$.
Limiting positions are often easier than calculus: here the parallel line cuts a similar triangle of ratio $\frac12$ (area $\frac14$ of the whole).
Open interval because $\theta=0$ (no point $M$) and $\theta=45^\circ$ (line through the apex, no quadrilateral) are excluded.

concepts: Distance between two points of intersection; range of a trigonometric expression
questions.paragraph: The base of an isosceles triangle is equal to $4$, the base angle is equal to $45^\circ$. A straight line cuts the extension of the base at a point $M$ at the angle $\theta$ and bisects the lateral side of the triangle which is nearest to $M$.
questions.question: The length of the portion of the straight line inside the triangle may lie in the range:
questions.key_idea: The portion inside the triangle is $PQ$; its length $\frac{2\sqrt{1+t^2}}{1+t}$ is monotonic on $t\in(0,1)$.
solution: Equation of line $PM$: $y-1=\tan\theta\,(x-1)$, with $P(1,1)$ on $AB$.
Its intersection $Q$ with $AC$ ($y=4-x$): $4-x-1=\tan\theta\,(x-1)$, so $Q\equiv\left(\frac{3+\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta},\frac{1+3\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}\right)$.
The portion inside the triangle is $PQ$, with $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\left(\frac{2}{1+t},\frac{2t}{1+t}\right)$ where $t=\tan\theta\in(0,1)$.
$\frac{2t}{(1+t)^2}$ is increasing on $(0,1)$ (its derivative is $\frac{2(1-t)}{(1+t)^3}>0$), so $PQ$ decreases.
As $t\to0^+$, $PQ\to2$; as $t\to1^-$, $PQ\to\frac{2\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt2$.
So $PQ\in(\sqrt2,2)$ (option C).

alternate_solutions.idea: In the right triangle $APQ$ (right angle at $A$) the hypotenuse is $PQ=\frac{AP}{\cos\angle APQ}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\cos(45^\circ-\theta)}$.
solution: $\angle A=90^\circ$, $AP=\sqrt2$ and $\angle APQ=45^\circ-\theta$ (from Q21).
$PQ=\frac{AP}{\cos(45^\circ-\theta)}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\cos(45^\circ-\theta)}$.
For $\theta\in(0,45^\circ)$ the angle $45^\circ-\theta$ runs through $(0,45^\circ)$ and its cosine through $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2},1\right)$.
So $PQ$ lies in $\left(\sqrt2,\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2/2}\right)=(\sqrt2,2)$ (matches); equivalently $PQ=\frac{2}{\sin\theta+\cos\theta}$.

useful_results: $\frac{2}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}=\frac{\sqrt2}{\cos(\theta-45^\circ)}$: a chord length through a fixed point often reduces to $\frac{\text{const}}{\cos(\theta-\varphi)}$, monotonic away from $\varphi$.
Ends of the range correspond to degenerate lines: $\theta\to0$ gives the parallel line $y=1$ (chord $2$), $\theta\to45^\circ$ gives the line $PA$ (chord $\sqrt2$).
The range is open at both ends because those two positions are excluded by the question.

Pair of straight lines
questions.question:
Match the following columns.
Column–I
(A) The four lines $3x-4y+11=0$; $3x-4y-9=0$; $4x+3y+3=0$ and $4x+3y-17=0$ enclose a figure which is
(B) The lines $2x+y=1$, $x+2y=1$, $2x+y=3$ and $x+2y=3$ form a figure which is
(C) If $O$ is the origin, $P$ is the intersection of the lines $2x^2-7xy+3y^2+5x+10y-25=0$, and $A$, $B$ are the points in which these lines are cut by the line $x+2y-5=0$, then the points $O,A,P,B$ (in some order) are the vertices of
Column–II
(P) A quadrilateral which is neither a parallelogram nor a trapezium nor a kite
(Q) A parallelogram which is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus
(R) A rhombus which is not a square
(S) A square
questions.key_idea: Equal distances between the two parallel pairs give a rhombus; perpendicular families make it a square; a pair of lines is first factorised.
solution: (A) $3x-4y+11=0$ and $3x-4y-9=0$ are parallel, with distance $d_1=\frac{|11+9|}{5}=4$; $4x+3y+3=0$ and $4x+3y-17=0$ are parallel, with distance $d_2=\frac{|3+17|}{5}=4$.
The normals $(3,-4)$ and $(4,3)$ satisfy $3\cdot4-4\cdot3=0$, so the two families are perpendicular and $d_1=d_2$: a square, (S).
(B) $2x+y=1$, $2x+y=3$ are parallel at distance $d_1=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}$; $x+2y=1$, $x+2y=3$ are parallel at distance $d_2=\frac2{\sqrt5}$.
$d_1=d_2$ but the normals $(2,1)$ and $(1,2)$ have dot product $4\neq0$, so the interior angle is not $90^\circ$: a rhombus that is not a square, (R).
(C) $2x^2-7xy+3y^2+5x+10y-25=(x-3y+5)(2x-y-5)$; the point of intersection of the two lines is $P(4,3)$.
The line $x+2y-5=0$ cuts $2x-y-5=0$ at $A(3,1)$ and $x-3y+5=0$ at $B(1,2)$; with $O(0,0)$: $m_{OA}=\frac13$, $m_{BP}=\frac13$, $m_{AP}=\frac21$, $m_{OB}=\frac21$.
So $OA\parallel BP$ and $AP\parallel OB$: a parallelogram. $m_{OA}\,m_{AP}=\frac23\neq-1$, so not a rectangle; $OA=\sqrt{10}\neq AP=\sqrt5$, so not a rhombus.
Hence (C) is a parallelogram which is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus, (Q). Answer: (A) S; (B) R; (C) Q.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute the vertices and test the diagonals: equal diagonals mean a rectangle, perpendicular diagonals mean a rhombus, both mean a square.
solution: (A) Vertices (intersections of consecutive lines): $\left(-\frac95,\frac75\right)$, $\left(\frac75,\frac{19}{5}\right)$, $\left(\frac{19}5,\frac35\right)$, $\left(\frac35,-\frac95\right)$; the diagonals join opposite ones: $\left(\frac{28}{5},-\frac45\right)$ and $\left(-\frac45,-\frac{28}{5}\right)$.
Both diagonals have length $\frac{\sqrt{800}}{5}=4\sqrt2$ and their dot product is $\frac{28(-4)+(-4)(-28)}{25}=0$: equal and perpendicular, a square (S).

(B) Vertices $\left(\frac13,\frac13\right)$, $\left(-\frac13,\frac53\right)$, $(1,1)$, $\left(\frac53,-\frac13\right)$; diagonals $\left(\frac23,\frac23\right)$ and $(2,-2)$ are perpendicular (dot product $0$) but of lengths $\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\neq2\sqrt2$: a rhombus, not a square (R).
(C) Parallelogram $OAPB$ with diagonals $\overrightarrow{OP}=(4,3)$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-2,1)$: dot product $-5\neq0$ (not a rhombus) and lengths $5\neq\sqrt5$ (not a rectangle): (Q).
Same matching: (A) S; (B) R; (C) Q.

useful_results: Two pairs of parallel lines make a parallelogram; it is a rhombus iff the two strip-widths are equal, a rectangle iff the families are perpendicular, a square iff both.
Equal diagonals $\iff$ rectangle; perpendicular diagonals $\iff$ rhombus (for a parallelogram); both $\iff$ square.
Pair of lines $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+\dots=0$ factorises as $(l_1x+m_1y+c_1)(l_2x+m_2y+c_2)$; the lines are perpendicular iff $a+b=0$.

(S) Lines are neither coincident nor concurrent
questions.key_idea: Concurrency means $\Delta=0$ and $\Delta=-(a+b+c)\left(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca\right)$, where the second factor vanishes only when $a=b=c$.
solution: $\Delta=\left|\begin{matrix}a&b&c\\b&c&a\\c&a&b\end{matrix}\right|$ and $\Delta=0$ is the condition of concurrency.
$\Delta=-(a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc)=-(a+b+c)\left(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca\right)$.
(A) $a+b+c=0$ but $\sum a^2\neq\sum ab$ (so $a,b,c$ are not all equal): $\Delta=0$, hence the lines are concurrent, (Q).
(B) $a+b+c=0$ and $\sum a^2=\sum ab\Rightarrow a=b=c\Rightarrow a=b=c=0$: every equation is $0x+0y+0=0$, satisfied by every $(x,y)$: the entire $xy$ plane, (P).

(C) $a+b+c

eq0$: the equations represent lines that are neither coincident nor concurrent, (S).
(D) $a+b+c\neq0$ and $\sum a^2=\sum ab\Rightarrow a=b=c\neq0$: the three equations all reduce to $x+y+1=0$, so the lines are identical (coincident), (R).

alternate_solutions.idea: Add the three equations to get $(a+b+c)(x+y+1)=0$, then settle each case directly; for (C) show that a common point would force $x^3=1$ and $a=b=c$.
solution: Adding the equations: $(a+b+c)(x+y+1)=0$. If $a+b+c=0$ the point $(1,1)$ satisfies all three, so the lines are concurrent: (A) $\to$ Q (they are distinct since coincidence needs $a=b=c$, which with $a+b+c=0$ is case B).
$a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca=\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]=0$ iff $a=b=c$; with $a+b+c=0$ this is $a=b=c=0$: all equations read $0=0$, giving the whole plane: (B) $\to$ P.
(D) $a=b=c\neq0$: each equation is $x+y+1=0$ after dividing by $a$: coincident, (R).
(C) Suppose a common point existed. Adding gives $x+y+1=0$ (as $a+b+c\neq0$), so $y=-1-x$. With $u=a-b$, $v=b-c$, $w=c-a$ the equations become $ux=v$, $vx=w$, $wx=u$.
Then $ux^3=u$. If $u\neq0$: $x=1$, so $u=v=w$, and $u+v+w=0$ gives $u=0$, a contradiction. If $u=0$ then $v=w=0$, i.e. $a=b=c$, excluded. So no common point: (C) $\to$ S (matches).

useful_results: Three lines $a_ix+b_iy+c_i=0$ are concurrent iff $\det(a_i,b_i,c_i)=0$ (or they are parallel in the degenerate case).
$a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)\cdot\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]$; the bracket is $0$ iff $a=b=c$.
For cyclic systems $ax+by+c,\ bx+cy+a,\ cx+ay+b$, summing the equations gives $(a+b+c)(x+y+1)=0$, so when $a+b+c=0$ the common point is $(1,1)$.

questions.key_idea: A trapezium with equal legs is cyclic; $ac=bd$ is the intercept (power-of-a-point) condition for four points on the axes to be concyclic.
solution: (A) $y=0$ and $y=1$ are parallel, so the figure is a trapezium. $x-6y+4=0$ meets them at $(-4,0)$ and $(2,1)$; $x+6y-9=0$ meets them at $(9,0)$ and $(3,1)$.
The legs are $\sqrt{6^2+1^2}=\sqrt{37}$ and $\sqrt{6^2+1^2}=\sqrt{37}$, equal, so it is an isosceles trapezium; hence it is also a cyclic quadrilateral: P, S.
(B) $ac=bd\Rightarrow\frac bc=\frac ad$. Taking the configuration of the figure, $\tan\theta=\frac bc$ with $\theta=\angle OCB$ and $\tan\phi=\frac ad$ with $\phi=\angle ODA$.
So $\theta=\phi$: the segment $AB$ subtends equal angles at $C$ and $D$, so $A,B,C,D$ are concyclic: a cyclic quadrilateral, P.

(C) For $ax\pm by\pm c=0$: if $y=0$ then $x=\pm\frac ca$; if $x=0$ then $y=\pm\frac cb$. The vertices $\left(\pm\frac ca,0\right)$, $\left(0,\pm\frac cb\right)$ form a figure whose diagonals (the axes) are perpendicular and bisect each other: a rhombus, Q.
The four lines form a square of side $4$ (width $6-2=4$, height $9-5=4$): a square, hence also a rhombus and a cyclic quadrilateral: P, Q, R.

alternate_solutions.idea: Symmetry for (A), and a circle-through-intercepts equation for (B): $ac=bd$ is exactly the condition that the circle through $A,C$ also meets the $y$-axis at $B,D$.
solution: (A) The reflection $x\to5-x$ keeps $y=0$, $y=1$ fixed and swaps $x-6y+4=0\leftrightarrow x+6y-9=0$ (since $5-x-6y+4=-(x+6y-9)$), so the figure is symmetric about $x=\frac52$: an isosceles trapezium, cyclic: P, S.
(B) A circle through $A(a,0)$ and $C(c,0)$ has the form $x^2+y^2-(a+c)x+ey+ac=0$ (at $y=0$ the roots are $a,c$).
Putting $x=0$: $y^2+ey+ac=0$, whose roots are $b,d$ exactly when $bd=ac$ (and $e=-(b+d)$). So $ac=bd$ puts $B$ and $D$ on that circle: P.
(C) The four vertices are symmetric about both axes, so the figure is a rhombus; it would be a square only if $|a|=|b|$, which is excluded, and it is not cyclic: Q only.
(D) Strip widths $4$ and $4$ with perpendicular lines give a square: P, Q, R (matches).

useful_results: A trapezium is cyclic iff it is isosceles (equal legs); a parallelogram is cyclic iff it is a rectangle; every square is a rhombus and cyclic.
Four points on two intersecting lines through $O$ (at signed positions $a,c$ on one and $b,d$ on the other) are concyclic iff $OA\cdot OC=OB\cdot OD$ (signed): power of the point $O$.
The lines $ax\pm by\pm c=0$ bound the rhombus with vertices $\left(\pm\frac ca,0\right),\left(0,\pm\frac cb\right)$; it is a square iff $a^2=b^2$ (the condition 'a\neq b' is read as $|a|\neq|b|$).
